lede: An enzyme is a protein that speeds up a reaction in a living thing. Warm it gently and it works faster; make it too hot, or too acidic, and it stops for good. That is why dough rises in a warm kitchen and why a high fever is dangerous.
can: Name the optimum and say what happens on each side of it.
Explain a rising rate by energy and collisions, and a falling rate by denaturation, in the words the mark scheme rewards.
Read the practical's graph the right way up: the shortest time is the fastest reaction.

md: Every enzyme has a temperature and a pH at which it works fastest, and on either side of that peak the rate falls away. The two falls are not the same thing, though: too cold only slows the enzyme down, while too hot pulls its shape apart for good. A question that says **explain** wants that difference.

md: The graph above is the shape every enzyme gives: the rate climbs, peaks, then falls away steeply. The peak is the **optimum**, the temperature at which the reaction runs fastest. The two sides look alike but happen for completely different reasons.

prompt: The temperature at which an enzyme works fastest is called its ______ .
explain: The optimum. CCEA's glossary defines it as the value of a factor that allows the reaction to happen at its fastest rate.

md: **Cold molecules move slowly.** The enzyme and the substrate have less energy, so they meet less often. Fewer collisions means fewer substrate molecules reaching an active site, so the rate is low. Nothing is damaged: warm the tube and the rate climbs back.

prompt: Why is an enzyme's rate low at 5 °C?
options: Fewer collisions between enzyme and substrate
The active site has changed shape
answer: Fewer collisions between enzyme and substrate
explain: Nothing is broken at low temperature — the molecules are simply slow. Denaturation only happens above the optimum.

md: Heat past the optimum and the enzyme molecule changes shape. The **active site** is the part that matters: once its shape has changed, the substrate is no longer complementary to it, cannot fit, and the reaction stops. The change is **irreversible** — that is what *denatured* means.

alt: Two enzymes side by side. On the left, at the optimum, the substrate's shape matches the notch of the active site. On the right, after heating, the notch is irregular and distorted, and a cross marks that the substrate can no longer fit into it.

Cooling will not undo it.</text><text x="246" y="138" font-size="11.5">heat</text></g></svg>
caption: The substrate has not changed. The active site has.

title: Why cooling does not bring it back
md: An enzyme is a long chain folded into one exact shape, and that folding is what makes the active site. Heat shakes the chain apart; as it cools it settles into some other folding, and the shape does not return.

prompt: An enzyme is heated to 70 °C, then cooled back to 37 °C. What happens to its rate?
options: It stays near zero, because the change is irreversible
It returns to what it was at 37 °C
answer: It stays near zero, because the change is irreversible
explain: Denaturation is permanent. This is the single most reliable way an exam distinguishes a memorised answer from an understood one.

md: Both sides arrive as one question about the graph at the top. **(a) Explain why the rate increases between 10 °C and 35 °C. [2] (b) Explain why the rate falls between 45 °C and 60 °C. [3]**
**1.** *As the temperature rises the molecules gain energy and move faster.* Start with what the heat does to the molecules; an answer that jumps straight to collisions has missed a mark.
**2.** *So there are more collisions between the enzyme and the substrate, and more enzyme-substrate complexes form.* That consequence is the second mark in part (a).

prompt: Part (b) opens “above the optimum the enzyme is denatured”. The change to the active site is then described as ______ .
explain: Irreversible. Cooling the enzyme does not fold it back, which is why the rate stays near zero.

md: **3.** *Above the optimum the enzyme is denatured.* Use that word: an enzyme is a molecule, so *killed* and *destroyed* are not on the accept list.
**4.** *The shape of the active site changes, irreversibly.* Which part changes, and that it cannot be undone: two separate ideas, and the pair is rewarded.
**5.** *The substrate is no longer complementary to the active site, so it cannot fit and the reaction stops.* Without it the answer describes a change but not a falling rate.

prompt: An enzyme with an optimum of pH 7 has almost no rate at pH 2. After “the enzyme is denatured”, what comes next?
options: The active site has changed shape, so the substrate no longer fits
The molecules are too slow to collide
answer: The active site has changed shape, so the substrate no longer fits
explain: The same ideas as part (b): the active site's shape, and the substrate no longer fitting.

md: **pH works the same way.** Every enzyme has an optimum pH as well as an optimum temperature, and either side of it the enzyme is denatured. The optima differ widely: a stomach enzyme near pH 2, a mouth enzyme near pH 7.

md: **Enzyme concentration is different:** nothing is damaged and there is no optimum. More enzyme means **more active sites available**, so more substrate is worked on at once and the rate rises, until every substrate molecule present is already in a complex.

prompt: The amount of amylase in a tube is doubled, at a fixed temperature. Why does the reaction speed up?
options: There are more active sites available
The enzyme has a higher optimum
answer: There are more active sites available
explain: More enzyme molecules, so more active sites, so more substrate molecules in a complex at any moment.

title: What the spec prints in bold
md: **Inhibitors are molecules that fit the active site but are not broken down.** The inhibitor occupies the active site, the substrate is blocked out and the rate falls. The enzyme is **not** denatured: its shape is unchanged.

alt: An enzyme with a molecule labelled inhibitor sitting inside its active site, and a separate substrate molecule outside marked with a cross to show it cannot get in.
svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 700 250" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-labelledby="k74t"><title id="k74t">An inhibitor molecule sitting in the active site, so the substrate is blocked out</title><g fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.8"><path d="M120 200 H240 V128 H212 L200 150 H160 L148 128 H120 Z"/><path d="M144 108 H216 L200 150 H160 Z"/><path d="M340 60 H412 L396 102 H356 Z"/></g><g stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" fill="none"><path d="M364 118 l24 24 M388 118 l-24 24"/></g><g font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="12.5" fill="currentColor"><text x="20" y="26" font-weight="600">Inhibitor (Higher Tier)</text><text x="256" y="140">inhibitor: it fits the active site</text><text x="256" y="156">but is not broken down</text><text x="332" y="196">substrate: blocked out,</text><text x="332" y="212">so the reaction rate falls</text><text x="20" y="238" font-size="12">The enzyme is not denatured — its shape is unchanged. The active site is simply occupied.</text></g></svg>
caption: Occupied, not damaged. That is the difference between an inhibitor and denaturation.

prompt: How does an inhibitor reduce an enzyme's rate?
options: It fits the active site but is not broken down, so the substrate is blocked out
It changes the shape of the active site permanently
It lowers the temperature of the reaction
answer: It fits the active site but is not broken down, so the substrate is blocked out
explain: The specification's own wording. Permanent shape change is denaturation, which is a different thing.

md: **The method.** Stand a tube of starch solution and a tube of amylase in the water bath until **both reach the bath temperature**, or the run is at the wrong temperature. Put iodine in each well of a spotting tile. Mix, start the stopwatch, and every 30 seconds move a drop into the next well. Iodine stays **blue-black** while starch is present; the first **yellow-brown** well gives the time. Repeat at each temperature.

prompt: Group A recorded 148 s and Group B recorded 152 s. The mean, in seconds, is
explain: (148 + 152) ÷ 2 = 150. Typing 148 + 152 ÷ 2 gives 224, because the calculator divides first — and a mean can never sit outside the two values.

md: **Read this graph the right way up.** It plots **time**, so the **shortest** time is the **fastest** reaction and the optimum is the **lowest** point, 40 °C here. Say 'the shortest time' when you justify it; 'the highest point' belongs to a rate graph.

prompt: From the results, the optimum temperature for this amylase, in °C, is
explain: 40 °C gave the shortest time, 60 s, so that is where the reaction was fastest.

md:
· Name the optimum and what happens either side of it.
· Below it: **fewer collisions**, and nothing damaged.
· Above it: **denatured** — the active site changes shape irreversibly and the substrate no longer fits.
· Say what more enzyme does, and what an inhibitor does.
· Read an optimum off a time graph.

Two factors, then the rise explained and the fall explained. In Booklet B it is the practical: times in seconds, a mean, a plotted graph, the optimum. The command words are Explain, Describe, Give a reason, Calculate, Plot and Suggest. Stuck: name the factor, say which way it moves the rate, then give the reason.
